source: A Tour of Pollis, page 3, Start by clicking, end with code you own.
context:
Every example runs as shipped
No, not to start. Fill in the boxes and run the example. Reading the code that Pollis writes is the easiest way to learn; changing it is the next step. Julia installs from the Welcome page. When a panel needs a package, Pollis installs it for you, with your agreement, in one click.

Each example comes with its own data: simulated, or a well-known real dataset from the companion package PollisDatasets.jl. Press Julia REPL and it runs. Then replace the example data with yours.

Not a black box Pollis is not a point-and-click statistics package that hides what it does. Every result comes with the code that produced it. You can read it, change it, rerun it and share it, so a colleague, a referee or a student can check exactly what was done. The path from menus to programming is a short one.
question: Do I need to know how to program to use Pollis?
answer: No, not to start: you fill in the boxes and run the example, and Pollis writes the code, which you can then read and change. Julia installs from the Welcome page, and Pollis installs the packages a panel needs, with your agreement, in one click.

Its code reads like the mathematics on the page and runs fast without being rewritten in another language, so the code a panel gives you is the code an expert would write. Work in progress

The name

question: Why does Pollis use Julia?
answer: Julia is free and open source and was designed for statistics, simulation and optimisation: its code reads like the mathematics and runs fast without being rewritten in another language, its packages work together, and it can call Python and R libraries when needed.

source: Pollis AI+, page 4, Voice Link: your own agent, on the road.
context:
2 Your agent works with Pollis: it opens the panels, runs the workflows and the Julia code it needs. 3 It writes it down: a dated note of what it did and found, saved in your Pollis Workspace. 4 You hear the answer: a short summary that your phone reads aloud. 5 You go on talking: a follow-up, a new idea, or “leave it for when I arrive”.

Why your own agent answers better than any chat A chat app on your phone knows nothing about your work: it can only give a general answer. Your agent at home sits in the middle of it. In your Pollis Workspace it finds your analyses, the panels and workflows you chose, your own menus, and your own panels, workflows and reports, structured and linked by you. So it answers about your data and your question, and it builds on what you have already done instead of starting again. And its numbers are not a model’s guesses: Pollis computes them in Julia, checked as everywhere else. The agent writes the words, not the results.

One idea, three places Voice Link is a Collaboration session, so others can join it: you on the road, your agent at home, and a colleague at their own computer, following the conversation, sharing code and adding ideas of their own. Their agent can join too. Pollis keeps it all in one place, ready for whoever picks it up next.
question: Why does Voice Link answer better than a chat app on my phone?
answer: Because your own agent at home works in your Pollis Workspace: it knows your analyses, panels, workflows and reports, and builds on them; and its numbers are computed by Pollis in Julia, not guessed by a model.

source: A Tour of Pollis AI+, page 5, Local Models › Which size?
context: A model’s size is its number of weights, written in billions: a “7B” model has about seven billion. Bigger is usually better, and needs more memory. A quantised model keeps each weight in fewer bits: a smaller file, slightly less accurate. The rule of thumb: the model’s file must fit in your computer’s memory, with room to spare for the conversation.
question: How do I know whether a model is too big for my computer?

source: A Tour of Pollis AI+, page 6, Embedding and Chat Models › What embeddings are for
context:
• Similarity: how close two texts are in meaning, as the cosine of the angle between their embeddings.
• Search: the passages of a corpus closest to a question, even when they use other words.
• Clustering: documents grouped by meaning, which gives topics.
• Features: numbers to put into a regression or a classifier, as any other variable. An embedding model is small, fast and steady: the same text gives the same numbers every time, with the same model. EmbeddingGemma 2, for example, has 271 million weights, where a chat model has billions.
question: What are embeddings used for?
answer: Similarity of meaning, as the cosine of the angle between embeddings; search of a corpus by meaning; clustering into topics; and features for a regression or a classifier.

source: Drill-down: Ask Pollis, page 5, The index › Words: the fts index
context:
DuckDB’s full-text search extension, fts, which comes with Pollis, indexes the heading and the text of each passage: PRAGMA create_fts_index('passages', 'id', 'heading', 'text', stemmer = 'english', overwrite = 1);

The English stemmer cuts words to their stems, so that filters finds filter and routing finds route. Common words (the, of ) are not indexed. The index takes a second or two to build.

answer: The fts index uses the English stemmer, which cuts words to their stems, so that routing finds route.

source: Drill-down: Ask Pollis, page 5, Finding the passages › One list
context:
The two lists are merged by reciprocal rank fusion: each passage scores 1/(60 + r) for its rank r in each list it is in, and the scores are added. A passage high in both comes first; a passage first in one list only still does well. The ranks are used, not the scores, because a BM25 score and a cosine distance are not on the same scale. In one query: WITH words AS ( SELECT id, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS r FROM (SELECT id, fts_main_passages.match_bm25(id, $question) AS score FROM passages) WHERE score IS NOT NULL ORDER BY r LIMIT 20), meaning AS ( SELECT id, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY array_cosine_distance(embedding, $vector::FLOAT[768])) AS r FROM passages ORDER BY r LIMIT 20) SELECT id, sum(1.0 / (60 + r)) AS score FROM (SELECT * FROM words UNION ALL SELECT * FROM meaning) GROUP BY id ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 8;

The best eight passages go to the model, about three thousand words in all. In a conversation, the question is searched together with the one before it, so that and on Windows? still finds the passages on installing an agent.
question: How does Ask Pollis merge the search by words and the search by meaning?
answer: By reciprocal rank fusion: each passage scores 1/(60 + r) for its rank r in each list it is in, and the scores are added; the best eight go to the model. Ranks are used because a BM25 score and a cosine distance are not on the same scale.

source: Drill-down: Ask Pollis, page 7, Comparing models › A test set, scored
context:
The questions of the test set are listed in a table, with each model’s rating in the run shown, sorted by any column. They come three ways:
• Made from the documents: Make Questions... takes 40 passages spread over the documents and has the model of the By field beside it, the default model unless you choose another, write for each a question that only that passage answers, and the answer. This is RAGTools.jl’s build_qa_evals. It is done once, and kept.
• Your own: Add takes a question, its right answer and the passage that holds it, chosen among those found for the question. Under an answer of Ask Pollis, Add to the Test Set... opens Add with the question and the answer, for you to correct, and the answer’s Sources to choose from.
• Imported: from a file of RAGTools.jl (below). Delete removes the questions ticked. The test set is a file of RAGTools.jl, evals.json: a JSON array of its QAEvalItem, each with four fields, source (the document and the place in it), context (the passage itself), question and answer, as JSON3.write saves them and JSON3.read(file,Vector\{QAEvalItem\}) reads them back. So a test set made elsewhere with RAGTools.jl can be run in Pollis, and one of Pollis read by anyone who uses RAGTools.jl: Import and Export take and give such a file.
question: In what format is the test set of Evaluate Models kept?
answer: evals.json, a file of RAGTools.jl: a JSON array of QAEvalItem, each with source, context, question and answer, so a test set can be imported from and exported to RAGTools.jl.

source: Drill-down: Ask Pollis, page 8, Keeping the index up to date › When it is built
context:
The index is built by the hidden process of low priority that compiles the documents of Help › Documentation when the Julia REPL starts, once they are compiled:
1. The passages and the fts index, from the documents that are new or changed since the last time, in a few seconds. This needs no model, and nothing is downloaded.
2. The embeddings of the new passages, the first time Ask Pollis is opened and every time after. The first time, this down-loads the embedding model, 0.31 GB, and computes every embedding, a few minutes on a laptop without a graphics chip; then only the new passages’, in seconds. The status bar shows Indexing the documentation for Ask Pollis, with the passages done.
question: How big is the embedding model that Ask Pollis downloads, and when is it downloaded?
answer: 0.31 GB, the first time Ask Pollis is opened; it then computes every embedding, which takes a few minutes on a laptop without a graphics chip.

source: Drill-down: Data Packages, page 2, The principle: Pollis's data is replaceable, yours never
context:
Three rules, and everything else follows from them.
1. What a package brings is a copy that an update may replace. Pollis never asks you to look after it.
2. What you do is written to files of yours that no update writes. They are JSON Lines, appended to and never rewritten: a change is a new line, and for each key the last line wins.
3. The five built-in databases are builds over both, read-only, rebuilt when what they come from changes. Deleting one loses nothing: it is made again at the next start of the Julia REPL.
question: How does Pollis keep what I do apart from the data its packages bring?
answer: What a package brings is a copy an update may replace; what you do is written to files of yours that no update writes, JSON Lines appended to and never rewritten, the last line winning for each key; the built-in databases are read-only builds over both.

context:
For a quote or a series, an alert can fire on what is unusual for it, rather than on a value you choose. • Leaves Its Band: the value leaves the band of so many standard deviations around its mean; once, until it is back within.
• Moves Beyond a Quantile: a move beyond that quantile, in per cent, of the moves before it; above 50 a rise, below 50 a fall.
• Makes a New High or Low: above the highest or below the lowest of so many Values Before It. The mean and the standard deviation weigh recent values more: Half-Life, in Values is after how many a value weighs half as much. The chart then shows what the alert would have done: its band over each minute of the last five days’ regular sessions, or over the series’ latest values, with a dot where it would have fired, and how many times. Change the numbers until it fires as rarely as you want.

context:
The Matrix A
- Full column rank for a unique answer. When columns are linearly dependent (more patterns than observations, or a pattern that is a combination of others), many x give the same fit, and the solver returns one of them.
- Overlap makes amounts uncertain. Columns that are nearly alike are hard to tell apart; NNLS then often gives all the weight to one of them and zero to the others, and which one can change with a little noise.
- No free intercept. A column of ones is constrained to be non-negative like any other. To fit an unconstrained baseline, subtract it from b first, or use a solver that leaves some coefficients free.

Scaling
Multiplying a column of A by a positive number divides its amount by the same number and leaves the fit unchanged, so the units of the columns do not change which components are zero. Flipping a column's sign does: the constraint is on the sign.

source: Novelty Detection, Novelty Detection › CUSUM
context:
The cumulative sum control chart (Page, 1954) monitors a series for a sustained shift in its mean. It adds up small deviations from the baseline, so a persistent change that is too small to see in any single observation still triggers an alarm.

Construction
```julia
using Statistics

mu0, sigma0 = mean(x_baseline), std(x_baseline)
z = (x_new .- mu0) ./ sigma0
k, h = 0.5, 5

S_up, S_down = zeros(length(z)), zeros(length(z))
for t in eachindex(z)
	S_up[t]   = max(0.0, (t == 1 ? 0.0 : S_up[t-1]) + z[t] - k)
	S_down[t] = max(0.0, (t == 1 ? 0.0 : S_down[t-1]) - z[t] - k)
end
alarms = findall((S_up .> h) .| (S_down .> h))
```

How It Works
Each step adds the standardised deviation minus an allowance k. While the process is in control the deviations are small and the sum keeps resetting to 0. After an upward shift it climbs steadily, and an alarm is raised when it exceeds h. The lower statistic does the same for downward shifts.
question: What does a CUSUM chart detect?
answer: A sustained shift in a series' mean: it adds up the standardised deviations minus an allowance k, and raises an alarm when the sum exceeds h, so a persistent change too small to see in one observation still triggers it.

source: Descriptive Statistics, Descriptive Statistics › Interpretation
context:
Centre
The mean is the balance point of the values; the median is the middle value. For symmetric data they agree. In right-skewed data (incomes, waiting times) the mean is pulled above the median by the long tail, and the median is the better "typical" value.

Spread
The standard deviation is in the units of the data. For roughly normal data, about two-thirds of the values lie within one standard deviation of the mean and about 95% within two. The interquartile range (Q3 - Q1) holds the middle half of the data and is not affected by outliers. The Percentile Report gives the full profile.
question: When is the median a better typical value than the mean?
answer: In skewed data, such as incomes or waiting times: the long tail pulls the mean above the median, and the median is the better typical value. For symmetric data they agree.

source: Proximity-Based Outlier Detection, Proximity-Based Outlier Detection › LOF
context:
The Local Outlier Factor (Breunig et al., 2000) compares the density around a point with the density around its neighbours. It measures whether a point is locally isolated, relative to its own region of the data.

Construction
```julia
using OutlierDetection, OutlierDetectionNeighbors
detector = LOFDetector(k = 10)
model, scores = OutlierDetection.fit(detector, permutedims(X); verbosity = 0)
```

How It Works
1. The reachability distance from p to a neighbour o is the larger of their distance and o's own k-distance, which smooths out tiny distances inside dense clusters.
2. The local reachability density of p is the inverse of its mean reachability distance to its k neighbours.
3. LOF is the average density of p's neighbours divided by p's own density.

Reading the Score
- About 1: as dense as its neighbours; a normal point.
- Clearly above 1 (say 1.5 or more): sparser than its neighbours; an outlier.
- Below 1: denser than its neighbours, typically the core of a cluster.

Strengths and Limits
- Handles clusters of different density, where KNN fails.
- Sensitive to k: too small gives noisy scores, too large merges nearby clusters. Check a range of values.
- Assumes roughly round neighbourhoods; for stretched clusters see COF.

See Also
- KNN · COF · Diagnostics
question: How do I read a Local Outlier Factor score?
answer: About 1: as dense as its neighbours, a normal point; clearly above 1, say 1.5 or more, sparser than its neighbours, an outlier; below 1, denser than its neighbours, typically the core of a cluster.

source: Net Survival & Competing Risks, Net Survival & Competing Risks › Interpretation
context:
Net Survival
"If the disease were the only cause of death, x% of patients would be alive 5 years after diagnosis." It removes the background mortality, so it compares groups with different life expectancy: countries, periods, men and women. It is not anyone's actual chance of survival; for a patient, use crude mortality.

Relative Survival
Observed survival divided by the survival expected from the rate table. The Observed, Expected and Relative Survival action shows the observed (Kaplan-Meier) survival, the expected survival (Ederer II), their ratio, and the net survival of the chosen estimator. Relative survival estimates net survival only when the excess hazard does not depend on age; Pohar-Perme does not need that.
question: Is net survival a patient's actual chance of survival?
answer: No: it is the survival if the disease were the only cause of death, which removes background mortality so that groups with different life expectancy can be compared. For a patient, use crude mortality.

source: Recurrent Neural Networks, Recurrent Neural Networks › Bidirectional RNNs › When You Cannot Use a Bidirectional RNN
context:
A BiRNN requires the entire sequence to be available at inference time. You cannot use it in any real-time or online setting:

Setting: Real-time trading signals; Why BiRNN is Excluded: Future prices are not yet known

Setting: Live speech-to-text; Why BiRNN is Excluded: Must transcribe as the speaker talks

Setting: Real-time fraud detection; Why BiRNN is Excluded: Cannot see future transactions

Setting: Autoregressive generation; Why BiRNN is Excluded: Output at step *t* is used as input at *t+1*

> Rule of thumb: if the entire sequence is available at inference time, a BiRNN will almost always outperform its unidirectional counterpart. If data arrives as a stream and you need immediate predictions, use a unidirectional RNN or a causal CNN.

---
question: Can I use a bidirectional RNN to make predictions in real time?
answer: No: a bidirectional RNN needs the whole sequence at inference time, so it cannot be used when data arrive as a stream and predictions are needed at once, as in live speech-to-text. Use a unidirectional RNN or a causal CNN.

source: State-Space Inference Methods, State-Space Inference Methods › Interpretation › Q and R: Trusting the Model or the Data
context:
The filter weighs the prediction against the measurement through the Kalman gain. What matters is the ratio of Q to R, more than either alone:

- Q large relative to R: the state is expected to move a lot, so each measurement pulls the estimate strongly. Estimates are responsive and noisy.
- Q small relative to R: the state is expected to be stable and measurements noisy, so the estimate follows the model and moves slowly. Estimates are smooth but lag behind real changes.

When Q and R are not known, the values that maximise the log-likelihood are the usual estimates.
question: What does the ratio of Q to R do in a Kalman filter?
answer: With Q large relative to R, each measurement pulls the estimate strongly: responsive and noisy. With Q small relative to R, the estimate follows the model: smooth, but lagging behind real changes. Unknown Q and R are usually the values that maximise the log-likelihood.

source: Time-to-Event Analysis, Time-to-Event Analysis › Diagnostics › Did the Fit Converge?
context: A fit has failed when its log-likelihood is lower than that of a model it contains (a Generalised Gamma below the Weibull), or when coefficients and standard errors are very large. LSurvival's own starting value for the Generalised Gamma, kappa = -10, is such a case, so the panel starts it from the Weibull's estimates, with kappa = 0: the Weibull itself.
question: Why does the Time-to-Event panel start the Generalised Gamma fit from the Weibull's estimates?
answer: Because LSurvival's own starting value, kappa = -10, makes the fit fail; the panel starts from the Weibull's estimates, with kappa = 0, the Weibull itself.

source: Bootstrap Resampling, Bootstrap Resampling › Confidence Intervals › BCa
context: Bias-corrected and accelerated (Efron, 1987): percentile endpoints moved by two corrections, z0 for the bias (the share of replicates below the estimate) and a, the acceleration, for a standard error that changes with the parameter (computed from the jackknife). It is second-order accurate: its coverage error shrinks faster with n than that of the percentile, basic and normal intervals. The usual default.
question: What is the BCa bootstrap interval?
answer: The bias-corrected and accelerated interval (Efron, 1987) moves the percentile endpoints by two corrections: z0 for the bias, the share of replicates below the estimate, and the acceleration a, computed from the jackknife, for a standard error that changes with the parameter. It is second-order accurate, its coverage error shrinking faster with n than that of the percentile, basic and normal intervals, and it is the usual default.

source: Cross-Validation Strategies, Cross-Validation Strategies › Assumptions › No Leakage
context:
- Everything learned from data happens inside the fold: scaling, imputation, feature selection, dimensionality reduction and tuning must be fitted on the training indices only. Fitting them on all rows first leaks information from the test folds, and the score becomes optimistic.
- No shared entities across train and test when the target is new entities, and no training on the future when the target is forecasting. The Leakage Check tests all three.
question: Can I standardise the features before cross-validating?
answer: Not on all rows first: scaling, imputation, feature selection, dimensionality reduction and tuning must be fitted on the training indices of each fold only. Fitting them on all rows leaks information from the test folds, and the score becomes optimistic.

source: Cross-Validation Strategies, Cross-Validation Strategies › Time-Series
context:
TimeSeriesSplit
TimeSeriesSplit makes k folds in time order: fold i trains on everything before block i + 1 and tests on block i + 1. By default the training window grows (expanding window); a maximum training size gives a rolling window, useful when old data are less relevant. A gap between training and test removes the observations right at the boundary, when features or targets span several periods. This is the strategy for forecasting: every fold predicts forward.

BlockedCV
BlockedCV divides the series into k contiguous blocks; each block is tested in turn, with all the others, before and after it, for training. A symmetric gap around the test block buffers against autocorrelation. It estimates performance across a dependent series, using all the data, but trains on the future, so it does not simulate forecasting.
question: What is the difference between TimeSeriesSplit and BlockedCV?
answer: TimeSeriesSplit trains on everything before each test block, with an expanding window by default or a rolling one with a maximum training size, so every fold predicts forward: it is the strategy for forecasting. BlockedCV tests each contiguous block in turn, training on all the others, before and after it, with a symmetric gap; it uses all the data but trains on the future, so it does not simulate forecasting.

source: Distribution Functions, Distribution Functions › Diagnostics
context:
Density and Cumulative Plots
The Density Plot shows where the probability lies: its centre, spread, skew and tails. The Cumulative Distribution Plot, drawn between the 0.1% and 99.9% quantiles, reads probabilities directly: the height at x is P(X <= x). Check that the shape is what you expect from the parameters; a surprising shape usually means a parametrisation mix-up.

Moments
Moments gives the mean, variance, skewness and (excess) kurtosis, or the mean vector and covariance matrix for vector-valued distributions. Skewness above about 1 in absolute value means a strongly asymmetric distribution; an excess kurtosis well above 0 means heavier tails than the normal.

Samples vs Density
Samples vs Density draws from the distribution and lays the histogram over the density. They should agree; disagreement points to a sampling problem or to a density that has not been normalised (a truncation or mixture set up wrongly).

Monte Carlo Check
The Monte Carlo Check compares the mean of many draws with the theoretical mean, with the Monte Carlo standard error. The difference should be within two or three standard errors. When the theoretical mean does not exist, the sample mean keeps jumping; this is the distribution's nature, not a bug.

Refit by Maximum Likelihood
Refit by Maximum Likelihood simulates data from the distribution and estimates its parameters back with fit_mle. The estimates should be close to the true parameters, closer as the sample grows. Large errors suggest parameters that are hard to identify from data of this size.
question: How do I check a distribution's mean by simulation?
answer: With the Monte Carlo Check, which compares the mean of many draws with the theoretical mean, with the Monte Carlo standard error: the difference should be within two or three standard errors. When the theoretical mean does not exist, the sample mean keeps jumping; this is the nature of the distribution, not a bug.

source: Distribution Sampling, Distribution Sampling › Diagnostics
context:
Sample Against Distribution
Sample Against Distribution lays the histogram of 10,000 draws over the density, or bars over the probability mass. For multivariate distributions it shows the first two components; for matrix-variate ones, the mean next to one draw. The histogram should follow the curve, with random fluctuations largest where the bins hold fewest draws.

Cumulative and Marginals
For univariate distributions, the empirical CDF of the sample against the exact CDF: the largest vertical gap between them is the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic. For multivariate ones, the histogram of each component; for matrix-variate ones, the distribution of the largest singular value.

Sample Against Exact Moments
The theoretical moments next to those of the sample. The sample mean should be within a few standard errors (the standard deviation over sqrt(n)) of the exact mean; higher moments, skewness and kurtosis, converge much more slowly. Where a moment is undefined, as the Cauchy mean, the exact value is NaN and the sample value meaningless.
question: Why does the kurtosis of my draws not match the exact value?
answer: Higher moments, skewness and kurtosis, converge much more slowly than the mean, which should be within a few standard errors (the standard deviation over sqrt(n)) of the exact mean. Where a moment is undefined, as the Cauchy mean, the exact value is NaN and the sample value meaningless.

source: Decision Tree Models, Decision Tree Models › Diagnostics
context:
Overfitting
Depth vs Accuracy plots the training accuracy and the 5-fold cross-validated accuracy as max_depth grows. The training accuracy keeps rising, towards a perfect fit; the cross-validated accuracy rises, levels off and then falls. Choose the depth where it levels off: beyond that the tree is learning noise. A large gap between the two curves at the chosen depth means the tree is still too complex, or the data too few.

Cross-Validation
Cross-Validation reports the k-fold accuracy (classification) or R-squared (regression), with its spread over the folds. A wide spread means the tree, and its score, depend strongly on which samples it saw: the high variance of single trees.

Confusion Matrix
The Confusion Matrix cross-tabulates predicted against true classes on the test set. Read the off-diagonal cells: which classes are confused with which. With unbalanced classes, overall accuracy hides a poorly predicted rare class; look at the recall of each class.

Stability
Refit on a slightly different sample (another split, a bootstrap sample). If the top splits change, the rules should not be read too literally; an ensemble, compared in Tree vs Random Forest, will be more reliable.
question: How do I choose the max_depth of a decision tree?
answer: With Depth vs Accuracy, which plots the training and the 5-fold cross-validated accuracy as max_depth grows: choose the depth where the cross-validated accuracy levels off, since beyond it the tree learns noise. A large gap between the two curves at that depth means the tree is still too complex, or the data too few.

source: First-Order Methods, First-Order Methods › Gradient Descent › Why It Zig-Zags
context: With an exact line search, each step ends where the new gradient is at right angles to the old direction, so successive steps are perpendicular. On a function whose contours are long thin ellipses, the gradient points across the valley rather than along it, and the iterates bounce from wall to wall, making slow progress along the floor. The worse the condition number kappa, the ratio of the largest to the smallest curvature, the slower the progress: the error shrinks by about ((kappa - 1) / (kappa + 1))^2 per iteration.
question: Why does gradient descent zig-zag?
answer: With an exact line search successive steps are perpendicular, and on long thin elliptical contours the gradient points across the valley rather than along it, so the iterates bounce from wall to wall. The worse the condition number kappa, the slower the progress: the error shrinks by about ((kappa - 1) / (kappa + 1))^2 per iteration.

source: Generalized Linear Models, Generalized Linear Models › Diagnostics
context:
Overdispersion
The Overdispersion Check divides the sum of squared Pearson residuals by the residual degrees of freedom. For a correct Poisson or Binomial count model it is about 1; well above 1, the counts vary more than the family allows and the standard errors are too small. Remedies: the Negative Binomial, or robust (HC) standard errors. The check does not apply to 0/1 data, nor to families that estimate their own dispersion (Gamma, Inverse Gaussian, Normal).

Fit
Fitted vs Observed should lie along the diagonal. The Deviance Analysis reports the deviance explained, 1 - residual deviance / null deviance, a pseudo R-squared: it is not comparable with the R-squared of a linear model, and is usually lower.

Model Comparison
The Likelihood Ratio Test compares the model with the intercept-only model: twice the gain in log-likelihood follows a chi-squared distribution with as many degrees of freedom as covariates. The Information Criteria (AIC, AICc, BIC) compare models of the same response, including different families; lower is better, and differences below about 2 are not meaningful.

Separation and Convergence
Very large coefficients with huge standard errors in a binary model mean separation: some combination of covariates predicts the outcome perfectly. Drop or merge the offending covariate, or use a penalised fit.
question: How do I know if my Poisson model is overdispersed?
answer: The Overdispersion Check divides the sum of squared Pearson residuals by the residual degrees of freedom: about 1 for a correct Poisson or Binomial count model; well above 1, the standard errors are too small. The remedies are the Negative Binomial or robust (HC) standard errors. It does not apply to 0/1 data, nor to families that estimate their own dispersion.

source: Generalized Linear Mixed-Effects Models, Generalized Linear Mixed-Effects Models › Interpretation › Conditional and Population-Averaged Effects
context: Under a nonlinear link, the effect within a group (conditional) is larger in absolute value than the effect averaged over the groups (marginal): averaging the S-shaped curves of the groups flattens them. The difference grows with the random-effect variance. Conditional vs Population Predictions shows predictions with each group's random effect against those with the random effects at zero; the spread between them is the effect of the groups.
question: Why is the effect in my logistic mixed model larger than the population-averaged one?
answer: Under a nonlinear link, the effect within a group (conditional) is larger in absolute value than the effect averaged over the groups (marginal), because averaging the groups' S-shaped curves flattens them. The difference grows with the random-effect variance; Conditional vs Population Predictions shows it.

source: Generalized Method of Moments (GMM), Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) › Diagnostics
context:
J-Statistic (Hansen Test)
The J-Statistic is n times the two-step objective, n g' S^-1 g, at the efficient estimate. Under the null that all moment conditions hold it is chi-square with degrees of freedom equal to the number of instruments minus the number of parameters. A small p-value means at least one instrument looks invalid, or the model is misspecified. A large p-value is consistent with valid instruments but cannot prove it: the test has low power, and assumes at least one set of valid instruments to begin with. It is the heteroskedasticity-robust version of the Sargan test. Not available when the model is just identified (J is zero).

First-Stage Analysis
The First-Stage Analysis gives, for each endogenous regressor, the partial F of the excluded instruments in its first-stage regression. The rule of thumb is F above 10; weaker instruments bias GMM toward OLS and make its standard errors unreliable.

Residual Diagnostics
Residual Diagnostics shows the structural residuals and the sample moments at the estimate. In an overidentified model they are not all zero; a moment far from zero relative to the others points to the instrument that disagrees.

Efficiency vs 2SLS
Efficiency vs 2SLS compares one-step GMM (2SLS) with two-step efficient GMM, both with robust standard errors. Under heteroskedasticity, two-step GMM should have smaller standard errors; if the estimates differ by much more than their standard errors, the instruments may identify different things, or the weight is poorly estimated.
question: What does a small p-value of the Hansen J test mean?
answer: That at least one instrument looks invalid, or the model is misspecified: under the null that all moment conditions hold, J is chi-square with degrees of freedom the number of instruments minus the number of parameters. A large p-value cannot prove the instruments valid, since the test has low power; and the test is not available when the model is just identified.

source: Hypothesis Testing, Hypothesis Testing › Interpretation › Effect Size
context: Effect Size reports how large the difference is in standard-deviation units: Cohen's d for one sample, Hedges' g for two, eta-squared (the share of variance explained by the groups) for several. Conventional guides for d are 0.2 small, 0.5 medium and 0.8 large, but what matters is the size in the units of the problem. With a large sample, a tiny effect is significant; with a small one, a large effect may not be.
question: My test is significant; how do I know if the effect is large?
answer: From the Effect Size, in standard-deviation units: Cohen's d for one sample, Hedges' g for two, eta-squared for several. The conventional guides for d are 0.2 small, 0.5 medium and 0.8 large, but what matters is the size in the units of the problem: with a large sample, a tiny effect is significant.

source: Penalised & Projection Regression, Penalised & Projection Regression › Diagnostics
context:
Coefficient Path
The Coefficient Path plots every coefficient against the L1 norm of the coefficient vector, from the strongest penalty (all zero) to the weakest. Predictors that enter early and stay are the strongest; coefficients that change sign along the path, or that enter and leave, point to correlated predictors competing.

Residuals vs Fitted
Residuals vs Fitted should show no structure. A curve means a nonlinear term or an interaction is missing; the penalty cannot supply it.

Selection Stability
Selection Stability refits the model on 100 bootstrap resamples and counts how often each predictor is selected. Predictors chosen in nearly every resample are reliable; those chosen in under half are not, and their presence in the selected model is close to chance. Two correlated predictors that each appear about half the time are usually substitutes for each other.

Bootstrap Coefficient Intervals
The Bootstrap Coefficient Intervals resample pairs (Bootstrap.jl), refit and report 95% percentile intervals with the share of resamples in which each coefficient is exactly zero. They show the variability of the penalised estimates; because of the shrinkage they are not confidence intervals for the true coefficients in the classical sense.

Cross-Validated RMSE
The Cross-Validated RMSE compares 5-fold prediction error with ordinary least squares on the same folds. A penalised model that does not beat OLS here gains nothing in prediction; with few predictors and many observations that is expected.

Observed vs Fitted
In Observed vs Fitted, shrinkage pulls the fitted values toward the mean: points flatter than the 45-degree line are the price of the lower variance.
question: How can I tell whether the lasso's selected predictors are reliable?
answer: With Selection Stability, which refits the model on 100 bootstrap resamples and counts how often each predictor is selected: those chosen in nearly every resample are reliable, those chosen in under half are close to chance. Two correlated predictors that each appear about half the time are usually substitutes for each other.

source: Linear Regression, Linear Regression › Diagnostics › Leverage and Influence
context:
- Leverage (the diagonal of the hat matrix, h_ii) measures how unusual an observation's predictors are. The average is p/n; above 2p/n is high.
- Cook's distance combines leverage and the size of the residual, and measures how much the fitted coefficients move when the observation is dropped. Values above 4/n, or clearly apart from the rest, deserve a look.
An influential point is not necessarily wrong: check it, and report the fit with and without it if it changes the conclusions.
question: When is an observation's leverage high in a linear regression?
answer: Above 2p/n: the leverage, the diagonal h_ii of the hat matrix, averages p/n. Cook's distance, which combines leverage and the size of the residual, deserves a look above 4/n. An influential point is not necessarily wrong: report the fit with and without it if it changes the conclusions.

source: Linear Mixed-Effects Models, Linear Mixed-Effects Models › Diagnostics
context:
Model Health Checks
Model Health Checks reports one problem per model:
- Mixed-Effects: a singular fit. A variance component estimated at zero, or a correlation of plus or minus 1, means the random-effects structure is richer than the data can support. Simplify it: drop the random slope, or the correlation between intercept and slope.
- Fixed-effects: convergence. The demeaning that absorbs the fixed effects is iterative; if it did not converge, the estimates are not reliable.
- IV: weak instruments. A first-stage Kleibergen-Paap F below about 10 means the instruments barely move the endogenous regressor, and the 2SLS estimate is biased toward OLS with unreliable standard errors.

Random-Effects Q-Q Plot
The Random-Effects Q-Q Plot compares the predicted random intercepts with the normal distribution the model assumes. A few groups far from the line are worth looking at; a clear S-shape or skew suggests a missing group-level predictor. The predictions are shrunk toward zero, so the plot looks less spread than the true effects.

Group Effects
The Group Effects plot (a caterpillar plot for the mixed model) shows each group's intercept with a 95% interval. Groups whose intervals overlap broadly differ little; a few outlying groups may deserve a closer look or a group-level predictor.

Hold-Out Prediction Error
The Hold-Out Prediction Error refits on 80% of the rows and computes the RMSE on the other 20%. An RMSE much larger than the in-sample residual standard deviation means overfitting. The mixed model predicts groups it has not seen at the population level, with their random effect at zero.
question: What does a singular fit mean in a mixed model?
answer: A variance component estimated at zero, or a correlation of plus or minus 1: the random-effects structure is richer than the data can support. Simplify it, by dropping the random slope or the correlation between intercept and slope.

source: Linear Programming, Linear Programming › Decision Guide › LP or MILP?
context:
1. Can the variables be fractional? If the quantities are large (tonnes, hours), an LP is usually enough, and its rounded solution close to optimal.
2. Are there logical conditions (either-or, at most k of these, a fixed cost if used)? Model them with binary variables: MILP.
3. Is the MILP slow? Look at the LP Relaxation Gap: tighter constraints (smaller big-M values, stronger bounds) make it smaller and the solve faster.
question: When do I need a MILP instead of an LP?
answer: When there are logical conditions, such as either-or, at most k of these, or a fixed cost if used, modelled with binary variables. If the quantities are large and can be fractional, an LP is usually enough. If the MILP is slow, tighter constraints (smaller big-M values, stronger bounds) make the LP Relaxation Gap smaller and the solve faster.

source: Linear Programming, Linear Programming › Duality › Complementary Slackness
context: At the optimum, for every constraint, either it is binding or its dual variable is 0: y_i (b_i - (A x)_i) = 0. And for every variable, either it is 0 or its dual constraint is binding: x_j ((A' y)_j - c_j) = 0. So a slack constraint has a zero shadow price, and a variable with a positive reduced cost stays at 0.
question: What is complementary slackness?
answer: At the optimum every constraint is either binding or has a zero dual variable, y_i (b_i - (A x)_i) = 0, and every variable is either 0 or has a binding dual constraint, x_j ((A' y)_j - c_j) = 0. So a slack constraint has a zero shadow price, and a variable with a positive reduced cost stays at 0.

source: Markov Chain Monte Carlo, Markov Chain Monte Carlo › Diagnostics
context:
Trace Plots
The Trace Plot shows the draws of each parameter against the iteration. A well-mixing chain looks like stationary noise around a constant level. Warning signs: a trend (the chain has not reached the target), long flat stretches (Metropolis-Hastings rejecting every proposal), slow wandering (high autocorrelation), or jumps between levels (several modes).

R-hat
R-hat, the potential scale reduction factor, compares the spread between chains (or between halves of one chain) with the spread within them. It approaches 1 as the chains converge to the same distribution. Values above 1.01 are a warning; run longer, or change the sampler or the parametrisation.

Effective Sample Size
The ESS is the number of independent draws that would give the same precision as the correlated chain. NUTS often reaches an ESS close to the number of draws; Metropolis-Hastings, a small fraction of it. Below about 100 per chain, estimates of the tails (interval endpoints) are unreliable.

Autocorrelation
The Autocorrelation plot gives the correlation between draws k steps apart. It should drop to near zero within a few lags. Slow decay means slow mixing, and is what lowers the ESS.
question: What R-hat value means my MCMC chains have not converged?
answer: Values above 1.01 are a warning: R-hat compares the spread between chains with the spread within them, and approaches 1 as they converge. Run longer, or change the sampler or the parametrisation.

source: Sampling-Based Bayesian Inference, Sampling-Based Bayesian Inference › Assumptions › The Priors
context:
- Priors are part of the model. The panel uses weakly informative priors: Normal(0, 10) for means and coefficients, Exponential(1) for standard deviations. They assume the data are on a scale of roughly units to tens; with data in thousands, rescale them or widen the priors.
- Proper priors. A prior that does not integrate to 1 can give an improper posterior, which no sampler can detect.
- Sensitivity. With many data the likelihood dominates; with few, the prior matters. Marginal Posteriors overlays prior and posterior to show which.
question: Which priors does the Bayesian inference panel use?
answer: Weakly informative priors: Normal(0, 10) for means and coefficients and Exponential(1) for standard deviations. They assume data on a scale of roughly units to tens; with data in thousands, rescale them or widen the priors.

source: Quasi-Newton Methods, Quasi-Newton Methods › Assumptions › The Curvature Condition
context: The BFGS update keeps H positive definite only if s'y > 0: the gradient increases along the step. On a convex function this always holds; on a non-convex one it is guaranteed by a line search that enforces the Wolfe conditions (HagerZhang, MoreThuente, StrongWolfe). BackTracking enforces only sufficient decrease, and Optim skips the BFGS update when s'y is not positive.
question: When does the BFGS update stay positive definite?
answer: Only if s'y > 0, the gradient increasing along the step. On a convex function this always holds; on a non-convex one a line search that enforces the Wolfe conditions (HagerZhang, MoreThuente, StrongWolfe) guarantees it. BackTracking enforces only sufficient decrease, and Optim skips the update when s'y is not positive.

source: Quasi-Newton Methods, Quasi-Newton Methods › Diagnostics › Gradient Check
context: The Gradient Check compares the automatic-differentiation gradient with a finite-difference one, at x0 and at the solution. The check uses central differences, accurate to about 1e-10 relative to the size of the gradient on a well-scaled f; differences of that order are normal (the forward differences the Derivatives option :finite uses are less accurate, about 1e-8); larger ones point to a non-smooth f or a mistake in a hand-coded gradient. At the solution both should be near zero.
question: How large a difference in the Gradient Check is normal?
answer: About 1e-10 relative to the size of the gradient on a well-scaled f, the accuracy of the central differences the check uses. Larger differences point to a non-smooth f or a mistake in a hand-coded gradient. At the solution both gradients should be near zero.

source: Quadratic Programming, Quadratic Programming › Interpretation › Dual Prices
context: The Dual Prices are the shadow prices of the constraints: the change in the optimal objective per unit change in a constraint's right-hand side. The price of the return constraint is the marginal variance of the last unit of required return, the slope of the frontier in variance; the price of the volatility cap is the marginal expected return per unit of extra squared volatility. A constraint that does not bind has a price of zero. Prices are local: they describe small changes, and change themselves when the set of binding constraints changes.
question: What do the dual prices of a portfolio QP mean?
answer: They are the shadow prices of the constraints, the change in the optimal objective per unit change in a constraint's right-hand side: for the return constraint, the marginal variance of the last unit of required return. A constraint that does not bind has a price of zero, and the prices are local, changing when the set of binding constraints changes.

source: Quadratic Programming, Quadratic Programming › Portfolio Optimisation
context:
Estimation Error
The optimiser treats mu and Sigma as known, but both are estimated, and it is drawn to the assets whose errors make them look best: mean-variance optimisation has been called an error maximiser. Expected returns are the hardest to estimate, and the optimal weights are very sensitive to them; covariances are estimated better, but with many assets the sample covariance is noisy and nearly singular. Remedies:
- Shrinkage of the covariance matrix towards a structured target (Ledoit and Wolf), or a factor model.
- Shrinkage of expected returns, or ignoring them: the minimum-variance portfolio depends only on Sigma.
- Constraints as regularisation: long-only and position limits act like shrinkage of the covariance matrix (Jagannathan and Ma, 2003).
- Resampling and robust optimisation, which optimise against a set of plausible inputs.
- Benchmarks: the equal-weight portfolio is hard to beat out of sample with estimated inputs (DeMiguel, Garlappi and Uppal, 2009), and the Benchmark Portfolios action compares the solution with it.

Risk Contributions
The Variance Attribution splits the portfolio variance into each asset's contribution. Risk parity portfolios choose the weights so that the contributions are equal, a different, non-quadratic problem.

Beyond Variance
Variance penalises gains and losses alike and suits roughly symmetric returns. Downside measures such as conditional value at risk lead to linear programmes over scenarios; utility-based formulations to general convex problems.

See Also
- QP · QCQP · MIQP
question: Why do mean-variance portfolios do badly out of sample?
answer: Because mu and Sigma are estimated, and the optimiser is drawn to the assets whose errors make them look best: it has been called an error maximiser, and the weights are very sensitive to the expected returns. Remedies are shrinking the covariance matrix (Ledoit and Wolf), the minimum-variance portfolio, which ignores expected returns, long-only and position limits, and resampling or robust optimisation; the equal-weight portfolio is hard to beat out of sample.

question: What does robust regression assume about the errors?
answer: Symmetric errors, for the robust fit to estimate the conditional mean: with skewed errors the M-estimate targets a centre between the mean and the median. It also needs a good robust scale estimate, and its asymptotic standard errors assume homoskedastic errors.

source: Sequential Monte Carlo, Sequential Monte Carlo › Diagnostics › Resampling and Path Degeneracy
context: The Resampling and Path Degeneracy traces the final particles back through their ancestors and counts the distinct ancestors at each earlier step. Each resampling step removes some lineages, so the paths stored by the filter coalesce: the early states are represented by few distinct particles, often a single one. This does not harm the filtering distribution at the current time, but makes the stored genealogy a poor estimate of the smoothing distribution of early states, which is why the smoother simulates backwards.
question: Why is a particle filter's stored genealogy poor for the early states?
answer: Each resampling step removes some lineages, so the stored paths coalesce and the early states are represented by few distinct particles, often a single one. This does not harm the filtering distribution at the current time, but it is why the smoother simulates backwards.

source: Sequential Monte Carlo, Sequential Monte Carlo › Resampling Schemes
context:
When to Resample
Resampling at every step adds noise and accelerates path degeneracy; never resampling (sequential importance sampling) lets the weights degenerate until one particle holds all the weight. Adaptive resampling resamples only when the ESS falls below a threshold times N; 0.5 is the common choice, and LowLevelParticleFilters defaults to 0.1. The Resampling Threshold Sweep compares 0, 0.1, 0.5 and 1 on the log-likelihood estimate.

Resampling and Smoothness
Resampling makes the likelihood estimate a discontinuous function of the model parameters, even with common random numbers, which hinders gradient-based or optimisation-based parameter estimation. Continuous resampling schemes, or methods that avoid differentiating through resampling, address this.

See Also
- Bootstrap Filter · Smoothing · Diagnostics
question: How often should a particle filter resample?
answer: Adaptively, only when the ESS falls below a threshold times N: resampling at every step adds noise and speeds path degeneracy, and never resampling lets one particle take all the weight. 0.5 is the common threshold; LowLevelParticleFilters defaults to 0.1.

source: Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS), Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS) › Diagnostics › First-Stage Strength

The classical rule of thumb is F above 10 (Staiger and Stock); recent work suggests much higher thresholds (around 100) for the usual t test to keep its size with robust errors. Below 10 the instruments are weak: the estimate is biased toward OLS and the confidence intervals are too narrow. Use the Anderson-Rubin interval.
question: What first-stage F statistic means my instruments are weak?
answer: Below 10, the classical rule of thumb (Staiger and Stock): the estimate is biased toward OLS and the confidence intervals are too narrow, so use the Anderson-Rubin interval. Recent work suggests much higher thresholds, around 100, for the usual t test to keep its size with robust errors.

source: Julia Manual, Functions › Dot Syntax for Vectorizing Functions
context:
In technical-computing languages, it is common to have "vectorized" versions of functions, which simply apply a given function f(x) to each element of an array A to yield a new array via f(A). This kind of syntax is convenient for data processing, but in other languages vectorization is also often required for performance: if loops are slow, the "vectorized" version of a function can call fast library code written in a low-level language. In Julia, vectorized functions are not required for performance, and indeed it is often beneficial to write your own loops (see Performance Tips), but they can still be convenient. Therefore, any Julia function f can be applied elementwise to any array (or other collection) with the syntax f.(A). For example, sin can be applied to all elements in the vector A like so:

julia> A = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]
3-element Vector{Float64}:
 1.0
 2.0
 3.0

julia> sin.(A)
3-element Vector{Float64}:
 0.8414709848078965
 0.9092974268256817
 0.1411200080598672

Of course, you can omit the dot if you write a specialized "vector" method of f, e.g. via f(A::AbstractArray) = map(f, A), and this is just as efficient as f.(A). The advantage of the f.(A) syntax is that which functions are vectorizable need not be decided upon in advance by the library writer.
question: How do I apply a function to every element of an array in Julia?
answer: With the dot syntax f.(A), which works for any function and any array or collection, such as sin.(A). Vectorized functions are a convenience in Julia, not needed for performance.

source: Julia Manual, Missing Values › Propagation of Missing Values
context:
missing values propagate automatically when passed to standard mathematical operators and functions. For these functions, uncertainty about the value of one of the operands induces uncertainty about the result. In practice, this means a math operation involving a missing value generally returns missing:

julia> missing + 1
missing

julia> "a" * missing
missing

julia> abs(missing)
missing

Since missing is a normal Julia object, this propagation rule only works for functions which have opted in to implement this behavior. This can be achieved by:

adding a specific method defined for arguments of type Missing,
accepting arguments of this type, and passing them to functions which propagate them (like standard math operators).

Packages should consider whether it makes sense to propagate missing values when defining new functions, and define methods appropriately if this is the case. Passing a missing value to a function which does not have a method accepting arguments of type Missing throws a MethodError, just like for any other type.

Functions that do not propagate missing values can be made to do so by wrapping them in the passmissing function provided by the Missings.jl package. For example, f(x) becomes passmissing(f)(x).
question: What happens when I pass missing to a Julia function that does not accept it?
answer: It throws a MethodError. Wrapping the function in passmissing, from Missings.jl, makes it propagate missing: f(x) becomes passmissing(f)(x).

source: Julia Manual, Missing Values › Control Flow and Short-Circuiting Operators
context:
Control flow operators including if, while and the ternary operator x ? y : z do not allow for missing values. This is because of the uncertainty about whether the actual value would be true or false if we could observe it. This implies we do not know how the program should behave. In this case, a TypeError is thrown as soon as a missing value is encountered in this context:

julia> if missing
           println("here")
       end
ERROR: TypeError: non-boolean (Missing) used in boolean context

For the same reason, contrary to logical operators presented above, the short-circuiting boolean operators && and || do not allow for missing values in situations where the value of the operand determines whether the next operand is evaluated or not. For example:

julia> missing || false
ERROR: TypeError: non-boolean (Missing) used in boolean context

julia> missing && false
ERROR: TypeError: non-boolean (Missing) used in boolean context

julia> true && missing && false
ERROR: TypeError: non-boolean (Missing) used in boolean context

In contrast, there is no error thrown when the result can be determined without the missing values. This is the case when the code short-circuits before evaluating the missing operand, and when the missing operand is the last one:

julia> true && missing
missing

julia> false && missing
false
question: Why does if missing throw an error in Julia?
answer: Control flow does not allow missing, since it is not known whether the value would be true or false: a TypeError, non-boolean (Missing) used in boolean context, is thrown. && and || throw too, unless the result is known without the missing operand.

source: Julia Manual, Performance Tips › Avoid untyped global variables
context:
The value of an untyped global variable might change at any point, possibly leading to a change of its type. This makes it difficult for the compiler to optimize code using global variables. This also applies to type-valued variables, i.e. type aliases on the global level. Variables should be local, or passed as arguments to functions, whenever possible.

We find that global names are frequently constants, and declaring them as such greatly improves performance:

const DEFAULT_VAL = 0

If a non-constant global is known to always be of the same type, the type should be annotated; const globals need not be annotated because their type is inferred from their initialization value.

Uses of untyped globals can be optimized by annotating their types at the point of use:

global x = rand(1000)

function loop_over_global()
    s = 0.0
    for i in x::Vector{Float64}
        s += i
    end
    return s
end

Passing arguments to functions is better style. It leads to more reusable code and clarifies what the inputs and outputs are.

note: Note
All code in the REPL is evaluated in global scope, so a variable defined and assigned at top level will be a global variable. Variables defined at top level scope inside modules are also global.

In the following REPL session:

julia> x = 1.0
1.0

is equivalent to:

julia> global x = 1.0
1.0

so all the performance issues discussed previously apply.
question: Why are untyped global variables slow in Julia?
answer: Their value, and so their type, may change at any point, so the compiler cannot optimise code that uses them. Make variables local or pass them as arguments, declare constants with const, or annotate the type.

source: Julia Manual, Strings › Unicode and UTF-8
context:
Julia fully supports Unicode characters and strings. As discussed above, in character literals, Unicode code points can be represented using Unicode \u and \U escape sequences, as well as all the standard C escape sequences. These can likewise be used to write string literals:

julia> s = "\u2200 x \u2203 y"
"∀ x ∃ y"

Whether these Unicode characters are displayed as escapes or shown as special characters depends on your terminal's locale settings and its support for Unicode. String literals are encoded using the UTF-8 encoding. UTF-8 is a variable-width encoding, meaning that not all characters are encoded in the same number of bytes ("code units"). In UTF-8, ASCII characters — i.e. those with code points less than 0x80 (128) – are encoded as they are in ASCII, using a single byte, while code points 0x80 and above are encoded using multiple bytes — up to four per character.

String indices in Julia refer to code units (= bytes for UTF-8), the fixed-width building blocks that are used to encode arbitrary characters (code points). This means that not every index into a String is necessarily a valid index for a character. If you index into a string at such an invalid byte index, an error is thrown:

julia> s[1]
'∀': Unicode U+2200 (category Sm: Symbol, math)

julia> s[2]
ERROR: StringIndexError: invalid index [2], valid nearby indices [1]=>'∀', [4]=>' '
Stacktrace:
[...]

julia> s[3]
ERROR: StringIndexError: invalid index [3], valid nearby indices [1]=>'∀', [4]=>' '
Stacktrace:
[...]
question: Why does s[2] throw a StringIndexError in Julia?
answer: String indices refer to code units, bytes in UTF-8, and code points 0x80 and above take several bytes, up to four. So not every index is a valid character index, and indexing into the middle of a character throws a StringIndexError.

source: Julia Manual, Performance Tips › Write "type-stable" functions
context:
When possible, it helps to ensure that a function always returns a value of the same type. Consider the following definition:

pos(x) = x < 0 ? 0 : x

Although this seems innocent enough, the problem is that 0 is an integer (of type Int) and x might be of any type. Thus, depending on the value of x, this function might return a value of either of two types. This behavior is allowed, and may be desirable in some cases. But it can easily be fixed as follows:

pos(x) = x < 0 ? zero(x) : x

There is also a oneunit function, and a more general oftype(x, y) function, which returns y converted to the type of x.
question: What is a type-stable function in Julia?
answer: One that always returns a value of the same type. pos(x) = x < 0 ? 0 : x returns an Int or the type of x; pos(x) = x < 0 ? zero(x) : x fixes it. oneunit and oftype(x, y) help in the same way.

source: Julia Manual, Performance Tips › Access arrays in memory order, along columns
context:
Multidimensional arrays in Julia are stored in column-major order. This means that arrays are stacked one column at a time. This can be verified using the vec function or the syntax [:] as shown below (notice that the array is ordered [1 3 2 4], not [1 2 3 4]):

julia> x = [1 2; 3 4]
2×2 Matrix{Int64}:
 1  2
 3  4

julia> x[:]
4-element Vector{Int64}:
 1
 3
 2
 4

This convention for ordering arrays is common in many languages like Fortran, Matlab, and R (to name a few). The alternative to column-major ordering is row-major ordering, which is the convention adopted by C and Python (numpy) among other languages. Remembering the ordering of arrays can have significant performance effects when looping over arrays. A rule of thumb to keep in mind is that with column-major arrays, the first index changes most rapidly. Essentially this means that looping will be faster if the inner-most loop index is the first to appear in a slice expression. Keep in mind that indexing an array with : is an implicit loop that iteratively accesses all elements within a particular dimension; it can be faster to extract columns than rows, for example.
question: Should my inner loop run over the rows or the columns of a Julia matrix?
answer: Over the first index: Julia arrays are stored in column-major order, as in Fortran, Matlab and R, so the first index changes most rapidly. Looping is faster when the inner-most loop index is the first in the slice expression, and extracting columns can be faster than rows.

source: Julia Manual, Modules › Standalone using and import
context:
For interactive use, the most common way of loading a module is using ModuleName. This loads the code associated with ModuleName, and brings

the module name
and the elements of the export list into the surrounding global namespace.

Technically, the statement using ModuleName means that a module called ModuleName will be available for resolving names as needed. When a global variable is encountered that has no definition in the current module, the system will search for it among variables exported by ModuleName and use it if it is found there. This means that all uses of that global within the current module will resolve to the definition of that variable in ModuleName.

To load a module from a package, the statement using ModuleName can be used. To load a module from a locally defined module, a dot needs to be added before the module name like using .ModuleName.

To continue with our example,

julia> using .NiceStuff

would load the above code, making NiceStuff (the module name), DOG and nice available. Dog is not on the export list, but it can be accessed if the name is qualified with the module path (which here is just the module name) as NiceStuff.Dog.

Importantly, using ModuleName is the only form for which export lists matter at all.

In contrast,

julia> import .NiceStuff
question: What does using ModuleName make available in Julia?
answer: The module name and the names on its export list; other names are reached by qualifying them, as NiceStuff.Dog. A locally defined module needs a dot, using .ModuleName, and using is the only form for which export lists matter.

source: Julia Manual, Types › Parametric Composite Types
context:
Type parameters are introduced immediately after the type name, surrounded by curly braces:

julia> struct Point{T}
           x::T
           y::T
       end

This declaration defines a new parametric type, Point{T}, holding two "coordinates" of type T. What, one may ask, is T? Well, that's precisely the point of parametric types: it can be any type at all (or a value of any bits type, actually, although here it's clearly used as a type). Point{Float64} is a concrete type equivalent to the type defined by replacing T in the definition of Point with Float64. Thus, this single declaration actually declares an unlimited number of types: Point{Float64}, Point{AbstractString}, Point{Int64}, etc. Each of these is now a usable concrete type:

julia> Point{Float64}
Point{Float64}

julia> Point{AbstractString}
Point{AbstractString}

The type Point{Float64} is a point whose coordinates are 64-bit floating-point values, while the type Point{AbstractString} is a "point" whose "coordinates" are string objects (see Strings).

Point itself is also a valid type object, containing all instances Point{Float64}, Point{AbstractString}, etc. as subtypes:

julia> Point{Float64} <: Point
true

julia> Point{AbstractString} <: Point
true

Other types, of course, are not subtypes of it:

julia> Float64 <: Point
false

julia> AbstractString <: Point
false

Concrete Point types with different values of T are never subtypes of each other:

julia> Point{Float64} <: Point{Int64}
false

julia> Point{Float64} <: Point{Real}
false

warning: Warning
This last point is very important: even though Float64 <: Real we DO NOT have Point{Float64} <: Point{Real}.
question: Is Point{Float64} a subtype of Point{Real} in Julia?
answer: No: concrete Point types with different values of T are never subtypes of each other, even though Float64 <: Real. Both are subtypes of Point itself.

source: Julia Manual, Methods › Method Ambiguities
context:
It is possible to define a set of function methods such that there is no unique most specific method applicable to some combinations of arguments:

julia> g(x::Float64, y) = 2x + y
g (generic function with 1 method)

julia> g(x, y::Float64) = x + 2y
g (generic function with 2 methods)

julia> g(2.0, 3)
7.0

julia> g(2, 3.0)
8.0

julia> g(2.0, 3.0)
ERROR: MethodError: g(::Float64, ::Float64) is ambiguous.

Candidates:
  g(x, y::Float64)
    @ Main none:1
  g(x::Float64, y)
    @ Main none:1

Possible fix, define
  g(::Float64, ::Float64)

Stacktrace:
[...]

Here the call g(2.0, 3.0) could be handled by either the g(::Float64, ::Any) or the g(::Any, ::Float64) method. The order in which the methods are defined does not matter and neither is more specific than the other. In such cases, Julia raises a MethodError rather than arbitrarily picking a method. You can avoid method ambiguities by specifying an appropriate method for the intersection case:

julia> g(x::Float64, y::Float64) = 2x + 2y
g (generic function with 3 methods)

julia> g(2.0, 3)
7.0

julia> g(2, 3.0)
8.0

julia> g(2.0, 3.0)
10.0

It is recommended that the disambiguating method be defined first, since otherwise the ambiguity exists, if transiently, until the more specific method is defined.

In more complex cases, resolving method ambiguities involves a certain element of design; this topic is explored further below.
question: Why does Julia say my method call is ambiguous?
answer: No method is uniquely the most specific for the arguments, as with g(x::Float64, y) and g(x, y::Float64) called as g(2.0, 3.0): Julia raises a MethodError rather than pick one, whatever the order of definition. Define a method for the intersection, g(x::Float64, y::Float64), preferably first.
